note: Platform: private/closed Ethereum network. Tested only, not chosen.

quote: In addition to the prototype, we have tested other technologies on a smaller scale, such as OpenCBDC.
note: OpenCBDC tested on a smaller scale. The document does not state its ledger type.

quote: conclusions from the testing so far do not imply that the technology we have tested necessarily represents the most appropriate technology for the CBDC core infrastructure.
note: No technology choice made.

quote: it may be appropriate for CBDC to use several registries linked together through bridges.
note: Possible multi-registry design. Lesson from testing, not a choice.

quote: we believe it is premature to draw a conclusion about which technological solution for the core infrastructure of a potential Norwegian CBDC is most appropriate.
note: Explicitly undecided.

quote: Both in Norges Bank's project and internationally, particular attention is placed on a solution where CBDC are issued and distributed on blockchain-based solutions
note: Focus of attention, not a choice. Permissioned/permissionless not specified here.

quote: Responsibility for customer due diligence under Section 10 (1) (a) of the Anti-Money Laundering Act will, as is the case today, rest with the banks.
note: Summary of a legal review (Syrstad 2023). Customer due diligence by banks implies identity checks; wallet tier is not stated. Not a premise for F2.

quote: However, under Section 10(1)(b) and Section 21 it is unclear
note: Continues on p15: it is unclear who is responsible for transaction monitoring under the AML Act. No access route or data holder is named.

quote: who will be responsible for transaction monitoring. This must be resolved through legislative amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering Act.
note: The monitoring holder is unresolved, so no route can be set.

quote: responsibility for reporting to the tax authorities and customer due diligence measures pursuant to the Anti-Money Laundering Act.
note: Reporting responsibility to the tax authorities is raised as an open issue. The reporting party is not named.

quote: a registry/database and functionality for issuing, distributing, confiscation and settlement of CBDC.
note: The prototype includes a confiscation function. Not an adopted design, and its purpose versus AML is not stated.

quote: one must consider the possibility of CBDC being stored privately by end users (“self- custody”), or the possibility for only approved providers of storage services to be able to store CBDC for the end user.

quote: Among other things, privacy solutions and solutions for regulatory compliance can be further elucidated.
note: The only privacy reference. It names future testing only and gives no linkability design.

quote: Norges Bank should not have information about individuals' CBDC holdings or payments.
modality: conditional: if a retail CBDC were issued; listed as a rough draft design feature
note: Normative design feature. Section 4 calls the list a rough draft because Norges Bank decided a CBDC is not currently warranted, so this is an option, not a commitment.

quote: Likewise, it should not be possible for the central bank to monitor or control the CBDC holdings of individual account holders or CBDC payments.
note: Frames the matter as the CB being unable to monitor, not merely unwilling to use the data. Status is still option (rough draft).

quote: while Norges Bank will neither receive nor need detailed information about the public's holdings of means of payment or which payments they make.
modality: conditional: two-tier model with banks keeping customer contact
note: Rests on the two-tier division of roles.

quote: The two-tier model means that the central bank does not have direct customer contact, information about the identity of individual CBDC account holders or conducts CBDC transactions in the ledger.
note: Footnote 22. The same footnote says the ledger recording each owner's CBDC is held by the central bank. The CB holds the ledger but not the identity.

quote: The list of design features below must therefore be considered a rough draft that will have to be made more detailed should issuing a CBDC become relevant.
note: Establishes that all Section 4 design features are options, not adopted commitments. Applies equally to F8, F10 and F12.

quote: Retail CBDC based on the Hyperledger Besu technology can provide the central bank with sufficient control over the central bank money in the ledger without gaining access to personal data.
note: Test Case 1, sandbox result only. Text appears under the page-11 printed footer but the delimiter labels it DOC 6 PAGE 11. Also used for F12.

quote: partly for personal data protection considerations, it may be important that the central bank cannot access data related to individual customers' payments or CBDC holdings.
note: Test design rationale.

quote: Should the central bank have access to such data, it could also trigger Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (CFT)monitoring duties.
note: Gives the rationale for keeping the CB without personal data.

quote: In the solution, personal data are protected through pseudonymity 16, whereby end-users are represented by anonymised addresses in the ledger without a direct link to their identity.
modality: conditional: unless the address is linked to identity
note: Pseudonymous ledger in the sandbox. The CB holds no identity mapping, but the link is possible via banks or court orders (see F9).

quote: This applies to both historical and future transactions and applies regardless of whether access is through the central bank, participating banks or others with read access to the ledger.
modality: conditional: once the address-identity link is established
note: Once the link exists, the CB with read access sees the full history. This is conditional, not routine, so it bears on F9 rather than defeating F1=no.

quote: Personal data protection is ensured by the central bank having sole access to aggregated data, while detailed customer data remains protected by role-based access control.
note: Test Case 5 covers a tokenised securities shared ledger, not a retail payments design.

quote: The solution is designed so that customer information remains with banks, while the ledger only contains what was necessary to execute transfers of retail CBDC.
note: Premise (i): banks hold identity. Whether banks routinely see and link transactions is not explicit, so the §6.5 inference is incomplete.

quote: If the ledger address of an end-user can be linked to an identity – either through banks, court orders, technical leaks or data collocation – any participant with read access to the ledger would be able to view the entire transaction history related to this address.
note: Banks are named as a possible linking source and as having read access. This suggests PSP linkability but does not state it is routine.

quote: Based on the current corresponding division of roles between banks and central banks, in a CBDC solution, banks will also have the direct customer contact
note: Customer relationship alone is insufficient for F2 under §6.5.

quote: Know Your Customer (KYC), Countering the Financing of Terrorism (CTF) and Anti Money Laundering (AML) requirements for CBDC would be the same as for other payment services.
note: Same-rules statement. No public authority or data holder is named as the access route, so n/d per the F3 trap.

quote: Fifth, it must be clarified who is to be responsible for transaction monitoring under the Anti-Money Laundering Act with respect to CBDCs.
note: The responsible party for AML monitoring is explicitly left open.

quote: either through banks, court orders, technical leaks or data collocation
note: Court orders are mentioned as a way to link an address to identity in the test, but no legal route or holder is described.

quote: KYC and AML checks of CBDC users would have to be performed by banks or other market participants that offer wallets for CBDC storage and transactions to their customers.
note: KYC by wallet providers implies verified identity at onboarding.

quote: It must be straightforward for the public to acquire retail CBDC through online and mobile banking services and ATMs by debiting their own bank accounts.
note: Acquisition runs through the user's own bank account. No lower-identification route is mentioned anywhere in the document (relevant to the §6.6a premise).

quote: If the ledger address of an end-user can be linked to an identity – either through banks, court orders, technical leaks or data collocation – any participant with read access to the ledger would be able to view the entire transaction history related to this address.
modality: conditional: address-identity link via banks, court orders, leaks or data collocation
note: Retrospective re-identification of the whole history is possible once the link exists.

quote: Pseudonymity alone cannot prevent full retrospective access once the identity link has been established.
note: Sandbox finding.

quote: CBDC should not be programmable money, and programmability, if implemented, should be at the payment service level.
note: Rejects programmable money; any programmability would sit at the payment service level.

quote: It must be possible to use central bank money for payments in various settings. This is a basic principle and applies regardless of conditions relating to other events and terms.
note: Principle of unrestricted usability.

quote: Norges Bank is assessing whether the introduction of a central bank digital currency (CBDC) is appropriate to ensure that the Norwegian krone remains an efficient, attractive and secure means of payment in the future.
note: Stated aim of the exploration.

quote: Drivers behind this exploration include falling cash usage, the potential of new technologies, the emergence of new money and payment systems and insights drawn from CBDC work in other central banks.
note: Drivers of the exploration: falling cash use and new technologies (also bears on innovation).

quote: Drivers behind this exploration include falling cash usage, the potential of new technologies, the emergence of new money and payment systems
note: New technologies named as a driver.

quote: Norges Bank has placed particular emphasis on whether the introduction of a CBDC could promote innovation in payment services and whether it would be a suitable instrument to strengthen contingency arrangements in Norway's payment system.
note: Innovation and contingency are the two emphasised assessment criteria.

quote: Introducing a retail CBDC is not an appropriate measure at this stage to promote innovation that enhances effective and secure payment services.
note: Assessment that the objective is not served by a retail CBDC now. The objective itself remains stated.

quote: A presumed purpose of introducing CBDC was that it would boost innovation in the use of blockchain technology.
note: Presumed purpose of a CBDC.

quote: Payment solutions using retail CBDCs could enhance the payment system's contingency arrangements, but contingency considerations do not at present provide a decisive argument for
note: Resilience is assessed as an objective but judged not decisive now.

quote: Introducing a retail CBDC is not a suitable measure for financial inclusion in Norway.
note: Explicit rejection of inclusion as a rationale for Norway.

quote: Introducing a retail CBDC could become relevant if necessary national control over the payment system is at risk, but this is not currently the case.
modality: conditional: if national control over the payment system is at risk
note: National control over the payment system is a conditional, potential objective.

quote: It may also become relevant should global operators be expected to take a dominant position in the Norwegian payment system and sufficient national governance and control of the payment system is not possible.
note: Same conditional sovereignty rationale.

quote: Norges Bank has placed particular emphasis on whether the introduction of a CBDC could promote innovation in payment services and whether it would be a suitable instrument to strengthen contingency arrangements
note: Two criteria given joint emphasis, but no explicit ranking of a main objective. 'Unranked' is also defensible.

supports_value: innovation in payment services; contingency/resilience (emphasised assessment criteria)
quote: Norges Bank has placed particular emphasis on whether the introduction of a CBDC could promote innovation in payment services
note: These are emphases in the assessment, not a documented ranking.

quote: the introduction of either a retail or wholesale CBDC is currently not warranted.
note: Decision of 10 Dec 2025 not to introduce a CBDC now. This is context for all objective and design cells.

quote: The ledger for CBDC holdings and transactions should probably be based on blockchain technology.
note: Blockchain preferred but hedged ('probably').

quote: This exploration has therefore been based on the assumption that a Norwegian CBDC solution will be based on blockchain technology, which enables the use of smart contracts to automate payments.
note: Working assumption of the exploration.

quote: Should Norges Bank issue a CBDC solution on a ledger, the Bank must decide whether this ledger should be public or private.
note: Public versus private is not decided. Appears within the wholesale section but refers to 'a CBDC solution'.

quote: This suggests that the ledger for a Norwegian CBDC, at least initially, should be private and with better mechanisms so that Norges Bank can control access.
note: Leans toward a private, permissioned ledger.

quote: Test Case 1: Characteristics of the Hyperledger Besu technology in retail CBDC projects.
note: Platform: Hyperledger Besu, retail sandbox only (tested). Hyperledger Fabric was tested for wholesale.

quote: The test system consists of two sandboxes based on different blockchain or distributed ledger technologies (DLT 11).
note: Describes the sandbox test setup.

quote: the central bank must ensure that no other actors can issue and destroy CBDC, while at the same time the central bank has no access to information about individual customers’ payments with or holdings of CBDC.
note: Design premise of the retail CBDC sandbox test. It is not an adopted commitment, and the paper states it contains no recommendations.

quote: the aim was to explore how the central bank can obtain real-time, aggregated overviews of circulation, and holdings in the system without access to detailed customer data.
note: The CB was meant to see only aggregates in the tested retail design.

quote: The central bank does not have access to customer data and does not have responsibility for AML/KYC/CTF, but through its own roles it has access to aggregated overviews of circulation, holdings, and transaction activity on the ledger.
note: The CB has no customer data but sees ledger transaction activity on a pseudonymous ledger. Whether it can routinely link addresses to persons is not fully settled.

quote: The ledger itself contains only what is necessary to represent ownership and transfers of retail CBDC, while customer information and identity data remain at the banks and outside the ledger.
note: Identity data are held off-ledger by the banks. This is a tested design.

quote: However, this creates a structural privacy risk if ledger addresses can be linked to identity, as the full transaction history will then be visible.
modality: conditional: if ledger addresses are linked to identity
note: Pseudonymity caveat: anyone who links an address to an identity sees the full history. This qualifies reading F1 = no as absolute.

quote: Access control at the application level is not sufficient to handle traceability at the ledger level.
note: A technical finding that limits the privacy guarantees of the tested design.

quote: Privacy is mainly based on pseudonymity, which does not provide adequate protection if unauthorised parties can link addresses to identities.
modality: conditional: if addresses are linked to identities
note: Not a retail CBDC test, but the same Besu pseudonymity limitation applies.

quote: Further work should also address how requirements for anonymity and privacy can be better met, for example through layered architectures or the use of secondary layers (layer 2) above a core ledger.
note: Privacy design is left for further work and is not decided.

quote: Banks are responsible for customer onboarding and for linking customers to ledger addresses that are registered in the banks’ own account registers.
note: Banks hold the address-to-person mapping (premise i). The text does not state explicitly that banks routinely see the retail transaction records, so premises ii and iii are undocumented.

quote: The solution is designed so that customer information remains with the banks, while the ledger only contains what is necessary to carry out transfers of retail CBDC.
note: Identity data sit at the banks. Bank visibility of transactions is not stated.

quote: Banks are responsible for customer onboarding and for linking customers to ledger addresses that are registered in the banks’ own account registers. Only addresses approved by banks can hold and use retail CBDC.
note: Onboarding is bank-approved. Verified identity is implied but not stated verbatim, and this is a tested sandbox, not an adopted design.

quote: Various login mechanisms have been tested, including traditional login via external ID solutions and the use of digital wallets.
note: These are authentication options tested for login, not onboarding identity requirements.

quote: A CBDC may be necessary to ensure that NOK will continue to be a safe, efficient and attractive means of payment in the future too.
note: Strategy 25 objective quoted in a technical paper. It could also bear on cash_substitute_resilience, but cash is not mentioned. No ranking is given.

quote: The overall objective of the technical testing has been to obtain information relevant to assessing whether the introduction of CBDC based on blockchain technology will contribute to an efficient and secure payment system.
note: This is an objective of the testing, not a declared CBDC objective.

quote: The test also had an innovation objective: to explore whether bank deposits in tokenised form could enable new processes or use cases
note: This is the objective of one test case, not a declared institutional CBDC objective.

quote: The sandbox solution in this test case is based on Hyperledger Besu, which is a permissioned ledger compatible with the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
note: Platform: Hyperledger Besu for retail. This is a tested platform, not a choice.

quote: In test case 2, Hyperledger Fabric is used as a DLT platform to explore the properties of wholesale CBDC in an interbank settlement environment.
note: Platform: Hyperledger Fabric, used for wholesale only.

quote: The project was based on the premise that a CBDC solution should be based on blockchain technology so that the benefits of this technology could be utilised.
note: This is an investigative premise, not a decision. Permissioned vs permissionless is not fixed here; see p6.

quote: The ledger solutions tested in the project have not necessarily been shared or distributed between independent actors. The blockchain may just as well be centralised or partially distributed within a controlled and permissioned setup.
note: Clarifies that the tested ledgers were permissioned and possibly centralised.

quote: The report is a technical elaboration and supporting report to the project's final report11, and does not contain recommendations on the introduction of CBDC.
note: No ledger choice is made in this document.

quote: This can be compared to how such processes are handled in today’s payment systems, which raises the question of whether improvements to existing systems may be a better alternative than implementing a CBDC based on ledger technology.
note: Raises doubt about DLT relative to improving existing systems. Not a decision.

quote: an appropriate architecture will therefore involve a deliberate combination of on-chain and off-chain components.
note: Summary finding on on-/off-chain mix. It is not a ledger-type choice for the retail core.
